## Research question and scope

In my Python SUPPORT2 notebook, I examined survival prediction using Cox regression and Random Survival Forest. Here, I use R to ask a related question: **how are selected clinical characteristics associated with mortality, and how much confidence can I place in those estimates?** I focus on adjusted hazard ratios, model assumptions, nonlinear age effects, and sensitivity to missing data.

I reuse the **day-3 landmark training cohort** and the export containing 28 predictors after excluding `scoma` and `adlsc`. The event is observed death (`event = 1`), and `time` measures follow-up in days **after** the landmark. I keep the Python test set separate so that this exploratory work does not reuse the patients reserved for predictive evaluation. The R models use a smaller clinical subset of the exported predictors; this report compares the contributions of the two workflows rather than benchmarking the languages.

## Project contribution

The project combines **predictive modeling in Python** with **statistical interpretation in R** using SUPPORT2, a historical dataset of 9,105 seriously ill hospitalized patients. Python provides the prediction and validation workflow. R gives me a convenient way to investigate clinical associations, check assumptions, and examine uncertainty from missing measurements.

I follow the sequence **data quality → clinical summaries → model estimation → diagnostics → sensitivity analysis → interpretation**. Each step answers a question raised by the previous one. My aim is to show both what the fitted models suggest and where their conclusions need more work.

## Setup and study population

**Why I start here.** Before fitting any model, I check the cohort, outcome coding, and follow-up definition. The landmark includes patients observed beyond study day 3, and subtracting three days puts their follow-up on the same time scale. Reusing the existing split keeps the R and Python components aligned. It also means that these results describe the landmark training cohort rather than all SUPPORT2 patients.

The file `support2_trained.csv` must be beside this `.qmd` document. It can be exported from the Python notebook using:

```python
# Run this once in SUPPORT2.ipynb, not in the R report.

pd.concat([X_train_reduced, y_train], axis=1).to_csv(
    "support2_trained.csv", index=False
)
```

```{r}
#| label: setup
required <- c("survival", "ggplot2", "knitr")
missing_packages <- required[!vapply(required, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(missing_packages)) {
  stop("Missing R packages: ", paste(missing_packages, collapse = ", "),
       ". Install them into the R environment used by Quarto.")
}

library(survival)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)
library(splines)  # Provides natural cubic splines

format_p <- function(p) format.pval(p, digits = 3, eps = 0.001)
ph_table <- function(object) {
  tab <- data.frame(Term = rownames(object$table), object$table, row.names = NULL)
  tab$p <- format_p(tab$p)
  tab
}

input <- "support2_trained.csv"
if (!file.exists(input)) {
  stop("Cannot find '", input, "' beside this Quarto document. Export it from Python first.")
}
train <- read.csv(input, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

needed <- c("time", "event", "age", "sex", "dzclass", "num.co",
            "diabetes", "dementia", "meanbp", "crea", "alb")
stopifnot(all(needed %in% names(train)))
stopifnot(!anyNA(train[c("time", "event")]))
stopifnot(all(is.finite(train$time)), all(train$time > 0),
          all(train$event %in% c(0, 1)))

n_imported_predictors <- length(setdiff(names(train), c("time", "event")))
train$sex <- factor(train$sex)
train$dzclass <- factor(train$dzclass)
train$bp10 <- train$meanbp / 10  # HR per 10-unit increase in mean BP

cat("Training patients:", nrow(train), "\n")
cat("Observed deaths:", sum(train$event == 1), "\n")
cat("Right-censored:", sum(train$event == 0), "\n")
cat("Predictor columns in exported CSV:", n_imported_predictors, "\n")
```

**Interpretation.** The training cohort contains **`r format(nrow(train), big.mark = ",")` patients**, with **`r format(sum(train$event == 1), big.mark = ",")` observed deaths** and **`r format(sum(train$event == 0), big.mark = ",")` censored observations**. A censored observation means that death was not observed during that patient's follow-up; it does not establish what happened afterward. The estimates below apply to patients observed beyond study day 3 in this training partition.

## Clinical characteristics and data quality

**Why I check the data before modeling.** I need to understand who is represented in the cohort and which measurements are incomplete. Otherwise, a model could conceal differences in the patient groups or rely on a selected subset of patients without making that clear. I first report missingness using the recorded values, before any imputation.

```{r}
#| label: descriptive
clinical_vars <- c("age", "sex", "dzclass", "num.co", "diabetes",
                   "dementia", "meanbp", "crea", "alb")

missing <- data.frame(
  Variable = clinical_vars,
  N_missing = vapply(train[clinical_vars], function(x) sum(is.na(x)), integer(1)),
  Missing_pct = vapply(train[clinical_vars], function(x) mean(is.na(x)) * 100, numeric(1)),
  row.names = NULL
)
knitr::kable(missing, digits = 2, caption = "Missingness in selected clinical variables")
```

I then summarize the patients by diagnosis. Age, comorbidity burden, and missingness may differ between these groups, which helps explain why an unadjusted survival comparison and an adjusted model can give different impressions. I summarize age with its median and interquartile range, and comorbidity count with its median, so the description is less influenced by extreme observations.

```{r}
#| label: baseline-table

by_diagnosis <- lapply(split(train, train$dzclass), function(d) {
  data.frame(
    N = nrow(d),
    Deaths = sum(d$event == 1),
    Age_median = median(d$age, na.rm = TRUE),
    Age_IQR = IQR(d$age, na.rm = TRUE),
    Female_pct = mean(d$sex == "female", na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    Comorbidities_median = median(d$num.co, na.rm = TRUE),
    Diabetes_pct = mean(d$diabetes == 1, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    Albumin_missing_pct = mean(is.na(d$alb)) * 100
  )
})
clinical_table <- do.call(rbind, by_diagnosis)
clinical_table <- data.frame(Diagnosis = rownames(clinical_table),
                             clinical_table, row.names = NULL)
knitr::kable(clinical_table, digits = 1,
             caption = "Training-cohort characteristics by diagnostic category")
```

Before fitting the Cox models, I also flag measurements that deserve a source or unit check. These flags are prompts for review, not established cleaning rules. I leave the recorded values in place because I cannot justify replacing or excluding them from the available information.

```{r}
#| label: plausibility-audit
# Flags for review only; not automatic exclusions.
audit <- data.frame(
  Check = c("Mean arterial pressure <= 0", "Albumin > 6 (assuming g/dL)",
            "Albumin <= 0", "Creatinine <= 0"),
  N = c(sum(train$meanbp <= 0, na.rm = TRUE),
        sum(train$alb > 6, na.rm = TRUE),
        sum(train$alb <= 0, na.rm = TRUE),
        sum(train$crea <= 0, na.rm = TRUE))
)
knitr::kable(audit, caption = "Values requiring clinical or unit verification")
```

In this exported cohort, the median age is **`r round(median(train$age, na.rm = TRUE), 1)` years**, ARF/MOSF accounts for **`r round(mean(train$dzclass == "ARF/MOSF") * 100, 1)`%** of the patients, and albumin is missing for **`r round(mean(is.na(train$alb)) * 100, 1)`%**.

**Interpretation.** The amount of missing albumin makes a missing-data sensitivity analysis worthwhile. The high albumin values and zero mean blood pressure readings also need verification. I cannot determine their cause from this export, and they remain a limitation of the fitted models. The albumin cutoff assumes g/dL and is an illustrative review flag, not a validated SUPPORT2 exclusion rule.

## Unadjusted survival by diagnosis

**Why I begin with Kaplan–Meier curves.** Before adjusting for other characteristics, I want to see how survival differs across diagnostic groups and when those differences appear. Kaplan–Meier estimation accounts for right-censoring without imposing the Cox model's covariate structure. I display the first year to keep the comparison readable. Interpretation assumes that censoring is non-informative within each group.

```{r}
#| label: fig-survival-diagnosis
#| fig-cap: "Kaplan–Meier estimates by diagnostic category, first year after study day 3"
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
km_group <- survfit(Surv(time, event) ~ dzclass, data = train)
plot(km_group, col = seq_along(levels(train$dzclass)), lwd = 2,
     xlim = c(0, 365), ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "Days after day-3 landmark", ylab = "Estimated survival")
legend("topright", legend = levels(train$dzclass),
       col = seq_along(levels(train$dzclass)), lty = 1,
       bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

I use the log-rank test to assess whether the groups have the same survival distribution across the available follow-up. This is an overall comparison: it does not tell me that every pair of groups differs. I read it alongside the curves because crossing curves and changing differences over time can make a single test result an incomplete summary.

```{r}
#| label: diagnosis-logrank
logrank <- survdiff(Surv(time, event) ~ dzclass, data = train)
logrank_p <- pchisq(logrank$chisq, df = length(logrank$n) - 1,
                    lower.tail = FALSE)
knitr::kable(data.frame(Test = "Log-rank", Chi_square = logrank$chisq,
                        df = length(logrank$n) - 1, p_value = format_p(logrank_p)),
             digits = 4)
```

**Interpretation.** COPD/CHF/Cirrhosis has the highest estimated survival during the first year, while Coma shows the steepest early decline. Cancer survival falls below ARF/MOSF around day 100. The log-rank test indicates an overall difference between groups (χ² = **`r round(logrank$chisq, 2)`**, df = **`r length(logrank$n) - 1`**, p **`r format_p(logrank_p)`**). These differences are unadjusted and do not establish causal effects of diagnosis.

## Adjusted Cox regression: clinical associations

**Why I fit an adjusted model.** The diagnosis groups differ in more than their diagnosis. I use Cox regression to estimate associations while accounting for selected demographic and clinical characteristics at the same time. I include age, sex, diagnosis, comorbidity count, diabetes, dementia, mean blood pressure, and creatinine to cover several clinically relevant dimensions while keeping the model readable. This is an exploratory selection, not a claim that I have included every important confounder.

These variables have relatively little missingness, so a complete-case model gives me a starting point with limited sample loss. That practical choice does not establish that excluding incomplete observations is unbiased. I assess the much more incomplete albumin variable separately in the imputation section. I scale blood pressure by ten so its HR describes a more readable change than a single recorded unit.

This model differs from Python's penalized 28-feature Cox model. Its purpose is to examine adjusted associations, so I do not compare their coefficients or scores as though they were the same specification. An HR above 1 indicates a higher instantaneous death hazard conditional on the included covariates; an HR below 1 indicates a lower hazard. An HR is not a ratio of survival probabilities.

```{r}
#| label: cox-fit
cox_formula <- Surv(time, event) ~
  age + sex + dzclass + num.co + diabetes + dementia + bp10 + crea

train_cc <- train[complete.cases(train[all.vars(cox_formula)]), ]
cat("Complete-case patients:", nrow(train_cc), "of", nrow(train), "\n")

cox <- coxph(cox_formula, data = train_cc, ties = "efron", x = TRUE, model = TRUE)
cox_summary <- summary(cox)

hr <- data.frame(
  Term = rownames(cox_summary$coefficients),
  HR = cox_summary$conf.int[, "exp(coef)"],
  Lower_95 = cox_summary$conf.int[, "lower .95"],
  Upper_95 = cox_summary$conf.int[, "upper .95"],
  p_value = format_p(cox_summary$coefficients[, "Pr(>|z|)"]),
  row.names = NULL
)
knitr::kable(hr, digits = 3,
             caption = "Adjusted hazard ratios from the complete-case Cox model")
```

I display the HRs with their confidence intervals so that both the estimated association and its uncertainty are visible. The logarithmic axis treats ratios above and below 1 consistently, and the reference line marks an HR of 1.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cox-forest
#| fig-cap: "Adjusted Cox hazard ratios and 95% confidence intervals"
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
ggplot(hr, aes(x = HR, y = reorder(Term, HR))) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = Lower_95, xmax = Upper_95),
                orientation = "y", width = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Adjusted hazard ratio (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Clinical interpretation.** This model uses **`r format(nrow(train_cc), big.mark = ",")` complete cases**. Sex is compared with `r levels(train_cc$sex)[1]`, and diagnosis with `r levels(train_cc$dzclass)[1]`. Age is measured per year, comorbidity count per additional condition, and `bp10` per 10-unit increase in recorded mean blood pressure. Creatinine is interpreted per recorded unit, pending verification of the source units.

After adjustment, Coma and Cancer are associated with higher hazards than ARF/MOSF (HRs **`r round(exp(coef(cox)["dzclassComa"]), 2)`** and **`r round(exp(coef(cox)["dzclassCancer"]), 2)`**, respectively), while COPD/CHF/Cirrhosis has a lower hazard (HR **`r round(exp(coef(cox)["dzclassCOPD/CHF/Cirrhosis"]), 2)`**). Older age, male sex, additional comorbidities, and higher creatinine are associated with higher hazards. Diabetes and higher mean blood pressure are associated with lower hazards in this specification. Dementia shows no clear association, as its 95% confidence interval includes 1.

These are adjusted associations rather than causal effects. In particular, the diabetes estimate does not show that diabetes is protective. The interpretation depends on the model and the selected covariates, and a single HR can conceal an association that changes over follow-up. I therefore check proportional hazards next. The unresolved measurement flags also remain relevant to these estimates.

## Proportional-hazards assumption

**Why I check proportional hazards.** The fitted Cox model represents each association with a coefficient that is constant over follow-up. Before interpreting those HRs as constant effects, I need to check whether that assumption is reasonable. Scaled Schoenfeld residuals and the Grambsch–Therneau tests look for evidence that the coefficients change over time. I consider the global test and the individual terms together; an isolated small p-value can also arise when several tests are performed.

```{r}
#| label: ph-diagnostics
ph <- cox.zph(cox, transform = "rank")
knitr::kable(ph_table(ph),
             digits = 4, caption = "Proportional-hazards diagnostic tests")
```

I also plot the age residual diagnostic. A table can flag a departure, but the estimated coefficient curve helps me see its pattern over follow-up. Under proportional hazards, the underlying coefficient would be constant. The plot is a diagnostic estimate, and its p-value does not measure the clinical size of the departure.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ph-age
#| fig-cap: "Scaled Schoenfeld residual diagnostics for age"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
plot(ph, var = "age")
```

**Interpretation.** The global test provides strong evidence against proportional hazards (χ² = **`r round(ph$table["GLOBAL", "chisq"], 2)`**, p **`r format_p(ph$table["GLOBAL", "p"])`**). The individual tests also show evidence of departures for every tested covariate except dementia, with diagnosis producing the strongest signal. The non-horizontal age coefficient curve is consistent with the age association changing over follow-up. These findings limit how confidently I can summarize the associations with constant HRs.

**R's contribution here:** `cox.zph()` brings the term-level tests, global test, and residual plots into the same modeling workflow. Python's notebook also includes Schoenfeld tests; here, I use the diagnostics to motivate an alternative specification.

### Alternative specification: diagnosis-stratified Cox model

**Why I try diagnosis stratification.** Diagnosis has the strongest PH diagnostic signal, and the survival curves suggest that the differences between groups change over time. Stratification lets each diagnostic group have its own baseline hazard while the remaining covariate coefficients are shared across groups. This is a targeted sensitivity analysis: it addresses the diagnosis component without assuming that the other PH departures disappear. The trade-off is that the model no longer estimates diagnosis HRs.

```{r}
#| label: stratified-cox
cox_strat <- coxph(
  Surv(time, event) ~ age + sex + strata(dzclass) + num.co +
    diabetes + dementia + bp10 + crea,
  data = train_cc, ties = "efron", x = TRUE
)
ph_strat <- cox.zph(cox_strat, transform = "rank")
knitr::kable(ph_table(ph_strat),
             digits = 4,
             caption = "Proportional-hazards diagnostics after diagnosis stratification")
```

**Interpretation.** The stratified model's global test remains significant (χ² = **`r round(ph_strat$table["GLOBAL", "chisq"], 2)`**, p **`r format_p(ph_strat$table["GLOBAL", "p"])`**). Age, comorbidity count, diabetes, dementia, and mean blood pressure still show evidence of departures, while sex and creatinine show no clear departures in this specification. Separate diagnosis baselines therefore do not fully resolve the PH concerns. A model with time-dependent coefficients would be a reasonable next investigation, but I do not fit that extension in this report.


## Nonlinear age effect

**Why I check the form of the age association.** In my starting specification, age enters linearly on the **log-hazard** scale. That is a choice in this model, not a requirement of Cox regression. I use a natural cubic spline with three degrees of freedom to check whether a modest amount of curvature improves the fit. The spline contains the linear age specification as a special case, and both fits use the same patients and other covariates, so a likelihood-ratio comparison is appropriate.

This addresses a different question from the PH diagnostic: curvature across ages is not the same as a coefficient changing over follow-up. I compare the age forms within the original Cox specification to keep the change focused. Its unresolved PH departures still limit the strength of the inference.

```{r}
#| label: nonlinear-age
cox_spline <- update(cox, . ~ . - age + splines::ns(age, df = 3))
model_comparison <- anova(cox, cox_spline, test = "Chisq")
print(model_comparison)
```

I plot the fitted age association relative to age 65, a reference close to the cohort's median age. I keep the other covariates fixed and restrict the curve to the central 90% of observed ages to avoid letting sparse age extremes dominate the display. The band shows pointwise model-based uncertainty in the HR relative to that reference.

```{r}
#| label: fig-age-spline
#| fig-cap: "Estimated hazard ratio across age, relative to age 65; other covariates fixed"
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
# Hold other variables constant and vary age.
reference <- train_cc[1, all.vars(cox_formula)[-c(1, 2)], drop = FALSE]
# all.vars() begins with time, event: remove both to keep predictor columns.
reference$sex <- factor(levels(train_cc$sex)[1], levels = levels(train_cc$sex))
reference$dzclass <- factor(levels(train_cc$dzclass)[1], levels = levels(train_cc$dzclass))
for (v in c("num.co", "diabetes", "dementia", "bp10", "crea")) {
  reference[[v]] <- median(train_cc[[v]], na.rm = TRUE)
}
ages <- seq(quantile(train_cc$age, 0.05), quantile(train_cc$age, 0.95), length.out = 100)
new_patients <- reference[rep(1, length(ages)), , drop = FALSE]
new_patients$age <- as.numeric(ages)
ref_patient <- reference
ref_patient$age <- 65

# Evaluate the fitted spline basis consistently using the model's stored terms.
M <- model.matrix(cox_spline, data = new_patients)
M_ref <- model.matrix(cox_spline, data = ref_patient)
delta <- sweep(M, 2, M_ref[1, ], FUN = "-")
log_hr <- drop(delta %*% coef(cox_spline))
se <- sqrt(rowSums((delta %*% vcov(cox_spline)) * delta))
age_curve <- data.frame(
  age = ages,
  HR = exp(log_hr),
  Lower = exp(log_hr - 1.96 * se),
  Upper = exp(log_hr + 1.96 * se)
)

ggplot(age_curve, aes(age, HR)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Lower, ymax = Upper), alpha = 0.18) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Hazard ratio relative to age 65") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Interpretation.** The spline curve shows an increasing hazard with age relative to age 65. However, the likelihood-ratio test provides little evidence that the spline improves fit over a linear age term (χ² = **`r round(model_comparison[2, "Chisq"], 2)`**, df = **`r model_comparison[2, "Df"]`**, p = **`r format_p(model_comparison[2, "Pr(>|Chi|)"])`**). Retaining linear age is reasonable for this comparison, although it does not resolve the time-varying age effect identified by the PH diagnostics.

**R's contribution here:** formula-based model updates, likelihood-ratio comparison, and an effect curve with uncertainty make a modeling choice transparent. The analysis demonstrates a test and its interpretation even when a more flexible specification is not supported.

The confidence bands describe the fitted association under the model; they are not prediction intervals for individual patients. Even a significant spline test would not establish better prediction on new patients.

## Multiple-imputation sensitivity analysis

**Why I examine missing-data sensitivity.** Albumin is missing for a substantial share of the cohort. Including it only through complete-case analysis would exclude many patients and could change which patients the estimates represent. I therefore compare complete-case and multiply imputed Cox analyses using **the same predictors, including albumin**. Holding the model formula fixed makes it easier to examine the consequences of the missing-data strategy, although the two analyses necessarily use different amounts of patient information.

I include the observed event indicator and the Nelson–Aalen cumulative-hazard estimate in the imputation model so that the replacement covariate values can reflect their relationship with the survival outcome. Survival time and event status are **never imputed**. This follows the survival-informed approach of [White and Royston (2009)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19452569/). Including observed outcomes is appropriate for this inferential analysis; a prediction pipeline for new patients cannot use outcomes that are not yet known.

The analysis assumes that missingness can be explained by the variables in the imputation model—often called **missing at random**—and that the imputation models are adequate. I cannot establish those assumptions from the observed data alone. There is a further limitation here: the imputation strategy uses a PH-based approximation, while the earlier diagnostics show unresolved PH departures. I treat the pooled HRs as exploratory. Stronger inference, particularly from a model with time-dependent coefficients, would require an imputation approach that accommodates those effects. [Keogh and Morris (2018)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30014575/)

I use ten imputations and ten iterations as a manageable exploratory run, then inspect the sample sizes, pooled intervals, logged events, and chain plots. This is a starting diagnostic check, not proof that the imputation has converged or that the estimates are robust. Longer runs, more imputations, and comparisons of observed and imputed distributions would be needed for a more developed analysis.

`mice` is optional so the rest of the report can render even if it is not installed. Install the R package with `install.packages("mice")` in your active R environment and re-render to execute this section.

```{r}
#| label: multiple-imputation
#| results: asis
#| warning: true
mi_available <- requireNamespace("mice", quietly = TRUE)
if (!mi_available) {
  cat("Multiple imputation NOT RUN: install the R package 'mice' into the R environment used by Quarto.\n")
} else {
  mi_formula <- Surv(time, event) ~
    age + sex + dzclass + num.co + diabetes + dementia + bp10 + crea + alb
  mi_vars <- c("time", "event", "age", "sex", "dzclass", "num.co",
               "diabetes", "dementia", "bp10", "crea", "alb")
  mi_data <- train[mi_vars]
  mi_data$H0 <- mice::nelsonaalen(mi_data, time, event)

  cc_alb <- coxph(mi_formula,
                  data = mi_data[complete.cases(mi_data[all.vars(mi_formula)]), ],
                  ties = "efron")
  initial <- mice::mice(mi_data, maxit = 0, printFlag = FALSE)
  methods <- initial$method
  pred <- initial$predictorMatrix

  # Do not impute survival time, event status, or the derived cumulative hazard.
  methods[c("time", "event", "H0")] <- ""
  pred[, "time"] <- 0
  pred[, c("event", "H0")] <- 1
  pred[c("time", "event", "H0"), ] <- 0
  diag(pred) <- 0

  imp <- mice::mice(mi_data, m = 10, maxit = 10, method = methods,
                    predictorMatrix = pred, printFlag = FALSE, seed = 42)
  fits <- with(imp, survival::coxph(
    survival::Surv(time, event) ~
      age + sex + dzclass + num.co + diabetes + dementia + bp10 + crea + alb,
    ties = "efron"
  ))
  pooled <- mice::pool(fits)
  mi_hr <- summary(pooled, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE)

  cc_ci <- exp(confint(cc_alb))
  cc_hr <- data.frame(term = names(coef(cc_alb)),
                      CC_HR = exp(coef(cc_alb)),
                      CC_Lower_95 = cc_ci[, 1],
                      CC_Upper_95 = cc_ci[, 2],
                      row.names = NULL)
  low_col <- intersect(c("2.5 %", "conf.low"), names(mi_hr))[1]
  high_col <- intersect(c("97.5 %", "conf.high"), names(mi_hr))[1]
  if (is.na(low_col) || is.na(high_col)) {
    stop("Could not identify the pooled confidence-interval columns.")
  }
  mi_display <- mi_hr[, c("term", "estimate", low_col, high_col)]
  names(mi_display) <- c("term", "MI_HR", "MI_Lower_95", "MI_Upper_95")
  mi_compare <- merge(cc_hr, mi_display, by = "term", all = TRUE)
  mi_samples <- data.frame(
    Analysis = c("Complete case, including albumin", "Each imputed dataset"),
    Patients = c(cc_alb$n, fits$analyses[[1]]$n),
    Deaths = c(cc_alb$nevent, fits$analyses[[1]]$nevent)
  )
  cat("\n\n")
  print(knitr::kable(mi_samples, caption = "Analysis sample sizes"))
  cat("\n\n")
  cat("\n\n")
  print(knitr::kable(mi_compare, digits = 3,
        caption = "Complete-case vs survival-informed multiple-imputation hazard ratios"))
  cat("\n\n")

  imputed_vars <- names(methods)[methods != ""]
  print(knitr::kable(data.frame(Variable = imputed_vars,
                               Method = methods[imputed_vars]),
                     caption = "Methods used for incomplete covariates"))
  cat("\n\n")
  if (!is.null(imp$loggedEvents) && nrow(imp$loggedEvents)) {
    print(knitr::kable(imp$loggedEvents, caption = "Imputation events requiring review"))
    cat("\n\n")
  } else {
    cat("No imputation events were logged. This alone does not establish imputation validity.\n\n")
  }
  # Basic convergence check for multiply imputed variables.
  plot(imp)
}
```

**How I read this comparison.** I look at shifts in HRs alongside both sets of intervals and the number of patients retained. I also inspect the chain plots and any logged events for signs that the imputation needs attention. A change in an estimate is evidence of sensitivity to the analysis strategy, not evidence that one estimate is closer to the truth.

**Interpretation.** `r if (mi_available) { albumin_row <- mi_compare[mi_compare$term == "alb", ]; sprintf("The albumin HR is %.3f in complete cases and %.3f after multiple imputation (MI 95%% CI %.3f–%.3f). The complete-case analysis uses %s patients; each imputed analysis uses %s.", albumin_row$CC_HR, albumin_row$MI_HR, albumin_row$MI_Lower_95, albumin_row$MI_Upper_95, format(cc_alb$n, big.mark = ","), format(fits$analyses[[1]]$n, big.mark = ",")) } else { "The imputation analysis was not executed, so no empirical comparison is available." }` Similar albumin estimates do not imply that every association is stable: compare all rows, both sets of intervals, and the differing sample sizes.

**R's contribution here:** `mice` lets me fit the same model to several completed datasets and pool the coefficient estimates with their uncertainty. That extends the project's missing-data analysis beyond the single-value preprocessing used for prediction in Python.

## Comparison with the Python workflow

**Why I compare the workflows at this point.** I can now connect the tools to the questions they helped answer. My comparison is about the analysis I carried out: Python supports the existing prediction pipeline, while R supports this investigation of associations, assumptions, and missing-data sensitivity. I keep those different aims visible so that convenience in one workflow is not mistaken for an accuracy advantage of a language.

### What each workflow contributes

| Dimension | R companion | Existing Python SUPPORT2 notebook |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Main question | How are selected clinical characteristics associated with mortality, and how defensible are those estimates? | How well do patient characteristics predict survival? |
| Cox analysis | Adjusted HRs and intervals, term-level/global PH tests, diagnosis stratification, and an age-spline comparison | Penalized Cox prediction and a separate `lifelines` refit with Schoenfeld PH tests |
| Missing data | Complete-case analysis and survival-informed multiple imputation with pooled uncertainty | Training-only median/mode imputation and missingness indicators in predictive pipelines |
| Nonlinear modeling | Tests the functional form of age in an explanatory Cox model | Random Survival Forest captures nonlinearities and interactions for prediction |
| Evaluation | Assumption checks and missing-data sensitivity in the training cohort | Test-set discrimination, Brier scores, calibration, cross-validation, bootstrap uncertainty, and subgroup evaluation |
| Communication | Clinical summaries, effect estimates, plots, and interpretation in Quarto | Exploratory analysis, predictive figures, and model evaluation in Jupyter |

The Python diagnostic refit is a separate model from its scikit-survival prediction model; using different estimators and penalties does not establish numerical equivalence. Likewise, the eight-predictor-group R Cox model and Python's 28-feature reduced model answer different questions.

### R advantages demonstrated in this analysis

- **Compact statistical workflow.** `survival` brings Kaplan–Meier estimation, adjusted Cox modeling, residual diagnostics, and stratification into a consistent modeling interface.
- **Transparent model development.** Formula updates and nested model comparisons make the age-spline question easy to express and inspect.
- **Missing-data uncertainty.** `mice` supports repeated imputation and pooled inferential estimates, extending the project's treatment of missingness beyond single-value preprocessing.
- **Integrated clinical communication.** Quarto places tables, uncertainty plots, interpretation, and execution details together in a readable report.

These are workflow advantages in this project. Python's `lifelines` also supports HR uncertainty, diagnostics, stratification, and spline formulas, while Quarto supports both R and Python. The report demonstrates convenience and added analysis rather than exclusive language capabilities. See the [lifelines documentation](https://lifelines.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Survival%20Regression.html) and [Quarto computation documentation](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/computations/positron.html).

### R disadvantages and practical trade-offs in this project

- **Additional setup.** Maintaining R, Quarto, and packages such as `mice` adds environment and dependency work alongside the existing Python notebook. The imputation contribution is absent if its optional package is unavailable.
- **More integration work.** Exporting a CSV creates another handoff where column types, category labels, patient identity, and split provenance need checking. A separate patient-ID manifest would strengthen reproducibility.
- **More computation and diagnostics for imputation.** Multiple completed datasets require repeated model fitting and checks of chains, distributions, and missing-data assumptions. This added effort buys a different treatment of uncertainty; it is not automatically better prediction.
- **No predictive evaluation in this R component.** The existing Python pipeline already connects preprocessing, Cox/RSF fitting, and validation. This R report concentrates on inference; its scope does not demonstrate a weakness in R's ability to fit or validate predictive models.

**My choice for this project.** I use the existing Python pipeline for prediction and validation, and the R companion for clinical interpretation, assumption checks, and missing-data sensitivity. To compare accuracy, speed, or predictive performance across implementations, I would need matched models, preprocessing, cohorts, and evaluation rules. The current project instead shows what the two workflows contribute to a shared clinical analysis.

## Findings and demonstrated skills

**Why these steps matter together.** The useful outcome is an account of which modeling choices are supported and which remain uncertain. The R analysis identifies PH departures that diagnosis stratification does not fully resolve, finds limited support for extra age curvature in the selected specification, and examines sensitivity to missing-data strategy. Those results help me explain the limits of the fitted models rather than simply present their coefficients.

| Project skill | Evidence in the combined R/Python work |
|:--|:--|
| Survival analysis | Landmark cohort definition, event/censoring handling, Kaplan–Meier estimates, Cox regression, and Random Survival Forest |
| Statistical judgment | Assumption diagnostics, a stratified sensitivity model, a nested age-spline comparison, and qualified interpretation of HRs |
| Missing-data methods | Missingness audit, predictive imputation pipelines, and survival-informed multiple imputation with pooled intervals |
| Model evaluation | Python discrimination, Brier scores, calibration, cross-validation, and bootstrap uncertainty |
| Reproducible communication | Executable notebook and Quarto report with shared cohort definitions and recorded R package versions |

The project demonstrates analysis development and interpretation using historical observational data. Its results remain exploratory; they do not establish causal effects or clinical deployment readiness.

## Limitations and conclusion

- SUPPORT2 is historical observational data; adjusted hazard ratios are **associations**, not causal effects.
- Estimates are conditional on the day-3 landmark cohort and the variables available at that point.
- Physiological plausibility and unit consistency, especially for albumin and mean arterial pressure, need source-data verification.
- Complete-case analysis can change the represented patient population. Multiple imputation relies on a defensible missing-at-random assumption and adequate imputation models, with further convergence and sensitivity checks needed.
- PH departures remain unresolved. The pooled HRs also remain exploratory because the imputation strategy does not explicitly accommodate time-dependent coefficients.
- Kaplan–Meier estimation assumes non-informative censoring within groups; Cox interpretation also requires a defensible censoring assumption conditional on the modeled covariates.
- PH diagnostics and nonlinear-age tests must be **interpreted from the actual rendered outputs**; this document does not assume the model passes them.
- The R inferential Cox model is different from Python's regularized 28-feature predictive Cox model, so performance differences are not a controlled comparison between programming languages.
- Independent clinical validation remains outside the scope of the training-only R analysis.

**Conclusion.** Using R alongside my Python notebook helped me examine the survival models from two perspectives: their predictive performance and the assumptions behind their interpretation. The R analysis gives adjusted associations, but its diagnostics also show why those associations need caution. Diagnosis stratification leaves PH concerns, the age-spline comparison provides little support for extra curvature, and the imputation comparison adds an exploratory view of missing-data sensitivity. The project demonstrates model development, validation, and interpretation on historical clinical data. Further work on time-dependent effects, imputation compatibility, and external validation would be needed for stronger clinical conclusions.

**Why I record the environment.** Package versions can affect execution and numerical output. I include the R session details so that someone rerunning the report can identify the environment used. Reproducing the combined project also requires the training export and the Python notebook's split and preprocessing definitions.
